opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, especially when building foundation models.

The way I see it, it's not really an either-or choice. It's more of a layered approach. At the bottom, you want a model that's as general as possible. It has seen a huge variety of data, it understands the world broadly, it has good priors about how things look, how they move, how physics roughly works. That generality is valuable because it's very expensive to collect data for every single application. If every robotics company or every autonomous driving team has to train from scratch, that's a lot of wasted effort. So a general model amortizes that cost across everyone.

But a general model, on its own, is usually not good enough for a specific deployment. If you're building a robot that picks items in a warehouse, you care about very particular things: the lighting in that facility, the objects on those shelves, the precision of the gripper. The general model gives you a strong starting point, but you need to post-train or fine-tune it on your own data to get the reliability you need. In the real world, especially in physical AI, 90% accuracy is often not acceptable. You need something much closer to 100%, and that last stretch usually comes from specialization.

So I think of it like education for people. You first get a broad education. You learn language, math, science, common sense about the world. Then you go on and specialize to become a doctor or an engineer. Nobody would say we should skip general education and go straight to medical school, and nobody would say general education alone makes you a surgeon. You need both, and each makes the other more effective.

There's also a practical trade-off in terms of compute and latency. A huge general model might be too slow or too expensive to run on a robot or in a car. So another path is to use the big general model as a teacher, and then distill it into a smaller, specialized model that runs efficiently on the edge. You keep a lot of the knowledge, but you make it practical.

So my view is: invest heavily in generality at the foundation level, because that's where the scaling benefits are, and then make it very easy for developers to specialize on top of it. The goal for us is to make the general model a good platform, so that people building specific applications can focus on their own problem instead of reinventing the basics.

r001.rationale: The response advocates a general foundation followed by specialization, and mentions compute and latency trade-offs, but does not frame single-application optimization as choosing which other capabilities to give up.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day, because at NVIDIA we sit right at the boundary between the two.

Let me start with the general side. A foundation model that is good at everything is really a way of amortizing cost. Pretraining on internet-scale data is enormously expensive, and nobody wants to pay that bill for one narrow use case. So you train once, you capture as much of the structure of the world as you can, and then everybody downstream benefits. The second thing a general model gives you is transfer. When you ask it to do a new thing, it already has the priors. It knows what objects look like, how they move, how language refers to them. That is why general models tend to be more robust when the inputs drift away from what you expected. A narrow model is very good inside its box and falls apart the moment you step outside.

But here is the honest part. Almost nobody deploys the fully general model as-is for a real product. For physical AI, for robotics, for autonomous driving, the application has constraints a general model doesn't know about. Latency, memory on an embedded chip, a specific camera rig, a specific safety requirement. And the data distribution in a factory or a warehouse is nothing like the internet. So what we actually see in practice is a pipeline: you start from the general model, and then you specialize. Post-training, fine-tuning on domain data, distillation into something smaller that fits on the device.

So I don't really think of it as a trade-off where you pick one point on a line. I think of it as two stages with two different objectives. The general model's job is to be a good starting point and to generate knowledge, including synthetic data, for the specialist. The specialized model's job is to be reliable and cheap in one place. If you try to make a single model do both jobs you usually end up mediocre at both.

The mistake I see teams make is in which direction they go. Some people start narrow, collect a small dataset, train a small model, and then wonder why it never generalizes. That path is a dead end, because you can't add world knowledge later. The other mistake is to keep scaling the general model and hope the application problems solve themselves. They don't. You still have to do the engineering.

With Cosmos, for example, our philosophy was exactly this. Build the world foundation model to be general about physics and video, and then make it easy for a robotics company or a car company to adapt it. We don't expect them to use our model directly for their robot. We expect them to use it as the thing that makes their specialized model possible.

So my short answer is: generality is where you invest your compute, specialization is where you earn your reliability, and the real skill is designing the hand-off between them.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with a general model and specializing it for reliability, cost, and deployment constraints. It does not frame single-application optimization as choosing which other capabilities to give up.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you want to optimize for. If you’re building a general-purpose model, you want capabilities that transfer across many tasks. That gives you flexibility, especially when you don’t know exactly how people will use it. But for a particular application, you may care much more about latency, cost, and reliability on a narrow set of inputs. Being good at everything doesn’t automatically make a model the best choice for that application.

So I don’t necessarily see these as competing directions. You can start with a broadly capable model and then adapt it, or distill its capabilities into a smaller model for a specific use case. The important thing is to evaluate the system on what the user actually needs. Does the additional generality improve the experience enough to justify its cost? That’s where I would make the trade-off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses weighing generality against application-specific cost and performance, but it does not frame single-application optimization as choosing which other capabilities to give up.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on where you draw the boundary between the model and the system. A general model gives you a strong foundation: it can handle different tasks, and capabilities learned in one area may help in another. But for a particular application, you usually care about a much narrower set of requirements—accuracy, latency, cost, and reliability.

So I wouldn’t treat this as a choice between two extremes. You can start with a general model and then specialize it through fine-tuning, tools, or the way you build the application around it. If the task is well defined and you can measure success clearly, a smaller, specialized model may be the better solution. If the application needs to handle many kinds of requests, flexibility becomes more valuable.

The key is to evaluate the whole system against what the user actually needs. Being good at everything is useful, but it doesn’t automatically make a model the best choice for a specific product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specializing a model for a defined task and weighing flexibility against application needs, but it does not frame that strategy as choosing which other capabilities to give up.
